query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation during elevated‐temperature exposure in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy is primarily governed by selective oxidation-driven elemental segregation. Under oxidizing conditions, chromium and titanium diffuse to the surface to form an initially protective mixed oxide scale that becomes unstable and spalls over time, leading to localized depletion in these elements and subsequent microstructural degradation. In reducing environments this segregation and scale formation are significantly suppressed, thereby better preserving the alloy’s integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a retained fcc matrix and a characteristic columnar grain structure resulting from the AM process
generation.intervention: Expose otherwise identical samples to two distinct atmospheric treatments: one in an oxidizing gas (e.g., dry air) and the other in a reducing gas mixture (e.g., 5% H2 in N2) under controlled temperature and time conditions
generation.conditions: Temperature of approximately 900°C for 100 hours; one set in air (21% O2) and the other in a reducing atmosphere (5% H2 in N2) to simulate elevated-temperature service conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Formation (and eventual spallation) of a Cr/Ti-rich surface oxide scale that depletes these elements in the near-surface region and alters the local chemistry of the underlying fcc matrix
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures in oxidizing conditions, enhanced diffusion of Cr and Ti leads to rapid, selective oxidation at the surface, creating a transient, initially protective oxide scale. Over time, thermal stresses and chemical instability lead to scale spallation, causing elemental depletion at the surface and eventual degradation of mechanical performance. In contrast, reducing conditions limit this selective oxidation and preserve the original elemental distribution and microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, microstructural analysis will reveal a Cr/Ti-rich oxide layer that exhibits spallation and surface microcracking, which correlates with measurable decrements in fatigue and strength relative to the baseline. Under reducing conditions, little to no significant oxide scale forms, preserving the alloy’s microstructure and mechanical integrity relative to the oxidized specimens.
generation.baseline: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy showing a stable fcc matrix with high strength and fatigue performance
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies for exposures around 900°C and durations of approximately 100 hours in atmospheres with high oxygen partial pressure versus mildly reducing conditions; deviations outside these conditions (e.g., significantly lower temperatures or much shorter exposure times) may not follow the same mechanisms
generation.uncertainty: The kinetics of elemental segregation and the precise timing and extent of oxide scale spallation are uncertain. Additionally, variations in microstructural features due to the additive manufacturing process (e.g., defect density or grain structure variations) may also influence degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical AM specimens and expose them to 900°C for 100 hours under two different atmospheres: one oxidizing (air) and one reducing (5% H2 in N2). After exposure, conduct detailed surface and cross-sectional characterization using SEM coupled with EDS and XRD to assess oxide scale composition, thickness, and integrity. Perform fatigue and strength tests on the exposed samples to evaluate mechanical degradation.
measurements: Quantitative oxide scale composition and thickness (via SEM/EDS and XRD)
Elemental profiles near the surface (via TEM/EDS) to assess selective depletion
Mechanical properties (fatigue life, tensile strength) post-exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing treatment does not result in a discernibly different Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale (or scale spallation) compared to the reducing treatment, and if both conditions yield similar levels of mechanical performance degradation, then the hypothesis—that selective oxidation-driven elemental segregation governs degradation—will be falsified.
